newsitem.title: UK: Netanyahu, in Europe, defends Jerusalem policy.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu, in Europe, defends Jerusalem policy.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, sharply criticised by the PLO and Egypt over his peace policies, basked in a diplomatic honeymoon in Britain on the first day of a European tour.

In a meeting at 10 Downing Street, Netanyahu and British Prime Minister John Major noted their differences over the Israeli leader's policy towards Jewish settlements and the future of Arab East Jerusalem, a senior Israeli official said.
But both men avoided public confrontation when they appeared before the media on Tuesday.
"The bilateral relationship between Israel and the United Kingdom is in as good a shape today as I can ever remember it being," Major told reporters after more than an hour of talks.
Asked about Netanyahu's plans to expand Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank, a move Britain views as an obstacle to peace, Major said he spoke candidly to the Israeli leader -- in private.
"Our interest in the United Kingdom is trying to provide a rapprochement to problems, not adding to them," Major said.
A beaming Netanyahu said his reception had been "exceptionally cordial" and praised Major's "reasoned and perceptive comments about our efforts to pursue peace".
Netanyahu pointedly noted in his remarks that he had met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, a summit that paved the way for his three-day visit to Britain, France and Germany.

"We are going to have a meeting of the (Israel-PLO) steering committee this week to begin to discuss the outstanding issues in the interim agreement and once these are disposed of, we can move on to negotiations on a final settlement," he said.
Citing security concerns, Netanyahu has yet to implement a long-delayed Israeli pullout from the West Bank city of Hebron and has pledged to expand Jewish settlements.
That policy and Netanyahu's opposition to trading occupied Arab land for peace has drawn fire from the Palestinians and Egypt, Israel's first peace partner.
Palestinian anger flared on Tuesday after Israel opened a tunnel near Islam's third holiest site.

Palestinians clashed with police after workmen under cover of night and heavy police guard punched a second entrance through a stone wall to a tourist tunnel beside Jerusalem's Temple Mount, a site holy to Jews and Moslems.
Arafat called the tunnel a "crime" against the religious status quo in the disputed city, and a breach of the foundering Israeli-PLO peace accord.
In Cairo, the Arab League said Israel had enraged Moslems worldwide and risked triggering widespread unrest.
Netanyahu defended the move.
"(It is) a decision I am very proud that we are implementing," he told reporters on his plane.
"Whoever has been in the Wailing Wall tunnel -- I was there a year ago -- could not help but feel the emotion to the depths of his soul...we are touching the rock of our existence."
Stepping up criticism of Netanyahu, Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said in an interview published on Tuesday Israel's peace policies were misguided.

"Israel wants security without there being a Palestinian state or even effective autonomy, without complete withdrawal from the Golan or complete withdrawal from Lebanon. And then it wants peace? Obviously nonsense," he told the London-based Arabic newspaper Ashraq al-Awsat.
Ending his British visit on Wednesday, Netanyahu will meet opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair and former prime minister Margaret Thatcher.
He then flies to Paris for talks with President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe before travelling to Bonn on Thursday to meet Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
